source: Written for Wayword as a learner's guide; not part of the original dataset. Examples are dataset phrases.
intro: Spanish is very regular: five pure vowels and a handful of consonants to learn. The dataset uses neutral Latin American pronunciation.
reading: CAPITALS mark the stress. A written accent (á, é, í, ó, ú) always marks it too.
Vowels are short and pure: "oh" without the English glide to "ohw".

sounds.name: Tap vs trill
sounds.how: A single r between vowels is one quick tap, like the tt in American "butter". rr, and r at the start of a word, is a rolled trill.

sounds.name: J and soft G
sounds.how: A throaty h, from mild (Caribbean) to scraping (Spain). Lejos is "LEH-hos".

sounds.name: LL and Y
sounds.how: Both are y as in "yes" in most places. In Argentina and Uruguay they become sh or zh.

sounds.name: Silent H
sounds.how: h is always silent: hola is "OH-lah".

sounds.name: C and Z
sounds.how: z, and c before e or i, = s in Latin America. In most of Spain they're a soft th, so gracias sounds like "GRAH-thyas". Both are correct.

sounds.name: B and V
sounds.how: They sound the same: a b at the start, and a soft b with lips barely touching between vowels.

tips_source: "How it's said" tips are written for Wayword (not part of the dataset): how a Latin American speaker says the phrase at normal speed, next to the careful pronunciation line.

tips.how_are_you: Cómo and estás run together with no break between the o and the e: KOH-moh-es-TAS, said like one word.
tips.speak_english: The s of hablas joins onto inglés: AH-blah-seen-GLES.
tips.dont_speak_well: The h is silent, so no and hablo slide into each other, and the n of bien carries over onto español: noh-AH-bloh BYEH-nes-pah-NYOL, all in one breath.
tips.say_again: The d in puedes is soft, close to the th in "this": PWEH-thes reh-peh-TEER. Most d's between vowels sound like this.
tips.speak_slowly: The s of puedes joins onto hablar (the h is silent): PWEH-deh-sah-BLAR mas des-PAH-syoh.
tips.learning_language: The y of estoy starts the next syllable, and aprendiendo runs into español: es-TOH-yah-pren-DYEN-doh-es-pah-NYOL.
tips.where_is: The e at the end of dónde and the e at the start of está merge into one: DON-des-TAH.
tips.how_get: The g in llego is soft: between vowels the back of the tongue doesn't quite close, so it's a breathy g. Llego and a run together: KOH-moh YEH-goh-ah.
tips.coffee: The n of un sounds like ng before the k sound of café: oong kah-FEH.
tips.water: The g in agua is very soft, so it can sound almost like AH-wah. Keep a hint of g, but don't make it hard.
tips.where_from: The e at the end of dónde and the e of eres blend into one: deh DON-deh-res, said like a single word. The r is a single quick tap.
tips.live_here: The s of vives joins onto aquí: VEE-veh-sah-KEE. Both v's are a soft b.
tips.been_america: Every final s and z joins onto the next vowel, so the phrase becomes one chain: ah-ses-TAH-doh al-GOO-nah VEH-seh-nes-TAH-doh-soo-NEE-dos.
tips.love_languages: Matching vowels merge, and the r of aprender links onto idiomas: men-KAN-tah-pren-DEH-ree-DYOH-mas.
tips.really: The final d is very soft and often barely there: deh vehr-DAH. The v is a soft b.
tips.interesting: Qué and interesante blend at the start: kayn-teh-reh-SAN-teh.
tips.like_talking: Gusta and hablar share one a (the h is silent): meh GOOS-tah-BLAR kon-TEE-goh. The g in contigo is soft.
tips.very_helpful: Muy glides straight into amable, its y starting the next syllable: EH-res mwee-yah-MAH-bleh.
